name: Androstadienone / copulins claims

lead: Androstadienone is a steroid in male sweat and semen, and copulins are fatty acids in vaginal fluid. Both have been proposed as human pheromones, and androstadienone is sold as an additive in colognes marketed to raise attraction, while copulins are said to signal fertility.

Lab studies have reported small changes in women's mood, attention and cortisol after smelling androstadienone. Reviews say no pheromone has been shown to directly change human behavior, and researchers dispute this. In animals pheromones act through the vomeronasal organ; in humans its receptor genes are nonfunctional, and proponents point to other nasal receptors as a possible route, which remains unconfirmed.

paras: Users buy colognes or sprays with androstadienone added and wear them as a regular fragrance. Others discuss the compounds on forums as part of the broader idea of scent as an attraction signal.
No specific harms are documented for the compounds in fragrance use. The main caveat in the literature is that product marketing claims go beyond the published research.

chain: Sweat steroid or fatty acid exposure
angle.text: Forum posters and sellers cite androstadienone and copulins as chemicals that could shift mood or arousal and make someone more appealing. Lab studies report small mood effects, while behavior change toward the wearer has not been shown.

lead: Androstadienone is a steroid found in human sweat, semen and other body secretions, and copulins are a group of volatile fatty acids found in vaginal fluid. Both have been proposed as human pheromones, meaning chemical signals that could change the behavior or physiology of other people without conscious awareness.[1][2][3]

In appearance and attraction circles, the claim is that androstadienone, often sold as an additive in men's fragrances and sprays, makes the wearer more sexually attractive, while copulins are said to signal fertility. Wikipedia notes that androstadienone is marketed in fragrances on the premise that it raises sexual attraction.[1]

Published research has reported small effects of androstadienone on women's mood, attention to emotional information and cortisol levels in laboratory settings.[1] Reviews state that no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly change human behavior, and that human pheromone research is limited by small samples, publication bias and weak methods. Researchers disagree about this conclusion.[2]

paras: Androstadienone (androsta-4,16-dien-3-one) is a 16-androstene steroid made in the body from androstadienol. It can be converted by 5-alpha-reductase into androstenone, which in turn can become androstenol. It has no androgenic or anabolic hormone effects.[1][4]

Copulins are six short-chain fatty acids, with acetic acid among them, first described in the vaginal fluid of rhesus monkeys. In women, about a third have all six, and levels rise before ovulation. Because human ovulation is concealed, their function in people is unclear and may not be sexual.[3]

The word pheromone was introduced in 1959 by Peter Karlson and Martin Luscher, building on work such as Adolf Butenandt's identification of the silkworm attractant bombykol.[2] Androstenone was the first mammalian pheromone identified, in boar saliva, where it triggers a mating stance in sows and has been sold to farmers for timing artificial insemination.[4]

Human research followed, focusing on underarm steroids, vaginal acids and the vomeronasal organ. In 1978 Kirk-Smith reported that androstenol led people to rate photographs as warmer and friendlier, and in 1971 McClintock reported menstrual synchrony in women, a finding later questioned on methodological grounds.[2]

Grosser and colleagues (2000) reported that very small amounts of androstadienone reduced nervousness and negative feelings in women. Lundstrom and Olsson (2005) found mood effects in heterosexual women that depended on whether a male or female experimenter was present, without any overt behavior change. Hummer and McClintock (2009) reported that the compound shifted attention toward emotional information, and Wyart and colleagues (2007) reported that smelling it altered women's cortisol.[1]

Reviews note that the effects are mood or attention shifts rather than changes in mate choice, and that results are inconsistent between individuals and settings, with some studies finding no effect at all.[1][2]

A frequently cited objection is that the genes for vomeronasal receptors are nonfunctional pseudogenes in humans and the organ appears to regress in adults, so a mechanism for detecting pheromones is uncertain. Jacob (2005) is cited as a skeptical review.[1][2] Proponents point to trace amine-associated receptors in the nasal lining as a possible detector, and to a 2019 report that a putative pheromone affected men's sexual cognition.[2]
The statement that no human pheromone has been demonstrated is itself listed as disputed, and the overall status of human pheromones is described as speculative and controversial.[2]

No studies found testing androstadienone or copulins as agents for increasing attractiveness in real-world dating or mating. Laboratory studies of androstadienone and mood, attention and cortisol are described above.[1]

Some body spray advertisers state that their products contain human sexual pheromones that act as aphrodisiacs. The cited reviews say such marketing goes beyond what peer-reviewed studies have shown.[2]
